serpGaps: Ranking guides (heymarvin, ramotion, tenet, 925studios 2026 founders' guide) are organized by PRINCIPLE (clarity, consistency, feedback, minimalism) and lean on onboarding. None is organized by the SURFACE a paying customer uses each week. Our structure: 7 in-product surfaces, each with a weak-vs-strong teardown and one metric.
No ranking page gives a metric per surface. We pair every surface with the number that shows it is failing (no benchmarks invented; the reader fills in their own).

saasui.design (parent-topic owner) has separate pattern posts for permissions, settings, billing and usage limits, and never joins them. We connect roles and billing: in B2B the member who hits a plan limit often cannot upgrade, so the limit screen must route a request to the admin.

No ranking page mentions US cancellation rules. We give one paragraph on California's AB 2863 (same-medium cancellation for consumer subscriptions, contracts from July 1, 2025; online cancel for online sign-ups is older law) and the vacated FTC click-to-cancel rule (ROSCA still enforced), framed as design consequences, not legal advice.
Accessibility in dense SaaS screens is missing: WCAG 2.2 target size (24 × 24 CSS px) for row actions and icon buttons.

Guides stop at 'design good empty states' for first-run. We cover the empty, loading, partial, error and no-permission states a RETURNING user hits (filters with no results, deleted data, failed sync). First-run empty states are linked to the onboarding service.

No ranking page shows real in-product before/after work. We use TradeZella (dashboard widgets, mentor mode), Mass Media Co. (one order screen, live estimated cost) and Digno (3-level scores), with only the facts the case studies state.
The guides end with generic 'hire experts'. We end with a triage grid that tells a team which ONE surface to fix first, which matches the pillar fact that a project can start with one part.

contentModules.title: UX design for SaaS: a teardown of the 7 surfaces users live in
contentModules.subtitle: Onboarding gets a user in. Seven surfaces decide whether they stay: dashboards, roles and permissions, data tables, settings, plans and billing, system states and retention loops. Each one torn down, weak against strong, with the metric that shows it is failing.
contentModules.intro: Scope-subtraction opener (see variety.introStyle). Sentence 1 carries the keyword in Faizan's voice (keywordCarrier.primary). Sentence 2 subtracts: the hub's own deliverable list has 6 parts and sign-up and onboarding is only one of them, so most of what a subscriber pays for sits elsewhere (link 'SaaS design agency' to the hub = UP link 1, within the first 150 words). Sentence 3 names the 7 surfaces this post tears down and says the homepage and first-run flow are covered elsewhere (one sideways link to /blog/saas-homepage-design/ with anchor 'the promise your homepage makes'). Sentence 4: what the reader gets (a teardown per surface + a triage grid). No question opener, no statistic first, no hypothetical company, no blockquote, no definition sentence.

dataModules.what: 7 surfaces arranged around one product frame. Each tile: surface name, the job it does for a paying customer, the one metric that shows it failing. Text panel: table surface | job | metric.
Two wireframes side by side: 'every metric at once' vs 'status, change, next action'. 5 numbered callouts on the strong side. Text panel: the 5 callouts.
One project screen seen by admin, member and guest, plus a 4th frame: the no-permission state with 'request access from <admin name>'. Text panel: table role | sees | can do | when blocked.
NN/g's 4 table tasks × the pattern that serves each (filter bar + saved views, frozen header + identifier column, side panel, selection + batch toolbar) × the failure symptom. Text table, no image.

Dead-end limit banner vs a 4-part limit message (what stopped, what still works, cost to continue, who approves), with the member→admin request path. Text panel: ordered list of the 4 parts + the weak version in one line.
Rows: empty (never used), empty (filtered to nothing), loading, partial data, error/failed sync, no permission. Columns: what the user needs to know | the one action to offer. Text table.
7 surfaces as rows × 3 columns (symptom you can see, metric to pull, first fix); the reader marks each row red, amber or green. Text panel: the same table with an empty 'your rating' column.

outline.h2: Which in-product surfaces decide UX design for SaaS after onboarding?
outline.answerHint: **Seven in-product surfaces decide whether UX design for SaaS keeps a paying customer: the dashboard, roles and permissions, data tables, settings, plans and billing, system states and retention loops.** (Framework-first H2, not a definition.)
points: One sentence on why these surfaces and not principles: a subscriber pays every month for the weekly work, so each surface needs its own test. Use 'ux for saas' carrier here or in H2 8.
Surface map (visual 1) + astext table: surface | job | metric (eav 'surface → metric map').
'The SaaS UX design patterns below are grouped by surface, not by principle.' (only use of 'saas ux design').
One sentence that sign-up and first run are a separate service (forward reference; link comes in H2 7).
Bridge: 'The first screen a returning user sees is the dashboard, so start there.'

outline.h2: What should a SaaS dashboard answer before anything else?
outline.answerHint: **A SaaS dashboard should answer one question at a glance, 'is my work on track, and what do I do next?', before it shows any secondary metric.**
points: NN/g definition and preattentive point (eav 'dashboard'): bars and lines read faster than gauges and tables for status.

Weak vs strong teardown (visual 2 + astext): weak = every metric at once; strong = status, change since last visit, next action, drill-down on demand. Hub fact: 'Home screens that show status, usage and next actions instead of every metric at once' (rephrase, do not paste).

Mini proof: TradeZella (link /case-studies/tradezella/): crowded interface hid key metrics; compact widgets for win rate and profit factor; traders choose and arrange widgets; results +40% user interaction and +25% retention, stated as results of the whole dashboard redesign.
'saas ui ux design' carrier sentence fits here (interface layer only works when the question is right).
Keep it to one section: 'saas dashboard design' is reserved for a future post (blog-opportunities 'saas dashboard', 30/mo, TP 350). No chart-type catalog, no KPI list.
Bridge: 'A dashboard that is right for an admin can be wrong for a guest, which is the next surface.'

outline.h2: How should roles and permissions show up in a SaaS interface?
outline.answerHint: **Roles and permissions should change what each person sees and can do on the same screen, and a blocked action should explain why and offer a way to request access, never a dead end.**
points: NIST RBAC (eav 'roles and permissions'): permissions attach to roles, so the UI is designed per role, not per user.
Role lens triptych (visual 3 + astext table): admin / member / guest + no-permission state with request access.
Hide vs disable: hide modules a role can never use; disable with a reason when the user could get access. Show who the admin is.

Digno (link /case-studies/digno/): one score shown at 3 levels, organization, department, individual, with a personal page that explains the factors. Use as the example of role-level views; no revenue figures.
LEAD ANGLE 1 at the end of this section (see leadAngle).
Bridge: 'Roles decide which rows a person sees; the table decides whether they can work with them.'

outline.h2: How do SaaS data tables handle finding, comparing, editing and bulk actions?
outline.answerHint: **SaaS data tables work when they support the 4 jobs users bring to them: find records, compare them, open or edit one row, and act on many rows at once.**
points: NN/g 4 tasks (eav 'data table tasks'); readable identifier in the first column; side panel keeps the table in view.
Table task matrix (text table, data module 4).
Carbon batch toolbar appears on selection (eav 'batch actions'); saved views and filter bars for repeat work.
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8: row actions and icon buttons at 24 × 24 CSS px minimum or spaced (eav 'target size').

Mass Media Co. (link /case-studies/mass-media-co/): separate tools → one platform; order screen updates estimated cost as items are added; results 30% order processing efficiency and the error-rate line exactly as stated ('2+, reduced from 25%').
Bridge: 'Saved views and column choices live somewhere, and that somewhere is settings.'

outline.h2: Where do settings belong in UX design for SaaS?
outline.answerHint: **Settings in UX design for SaaS belong in three clearly separated places: personal preferences, workspace settings and admin controls, each no more than two levels deep.**
points: Progressive disclosure, 2 levels max (eav 'settings depth').

Personal (notifications, theme, profile) vs workspace (integrations, defaults) vs admin (members, roles, security, billing access). Settings search for products with many controls (method, no number).
Destructive actions (delete workspace, remove member): separated, confirmed with the object name, and reversible where possible (method).
Hub fact: 'Roles and settings' deliverable covers admin, member and guest views, permissions, integrations and audit logs (paraphrase in one clause, link only if not already linked).
Bridge: 'One setting every subscriber eventually opens is the plan, and that is where SaaS UX touches revenue.'

outline.h2: How should SaaS billing, plan limits and cancellation screens work?
outline.answerHint: **SaaS billing screens should show the current plan, usage against its limits and the next charge plainly, turn a limit into a clear choice, and let people cancel the way they signed up.**
points: Plan-limit message anatomy (visual 5 + astext ol): what stopped, what still works, cost to continue, who approves (eav 'plan-limit message order'). Usage meter BEFORE the limit (warn early).
B2B twist in one sentence: the member who hits the limit often cannot pay; route a request to the admin (forward-links H2 9).
Invoice history and payment method as the reassurance layer (method).

US rules as design consequences (eav 'cancellation' rows): California AB 2863 for consumer subscriptions (same-medium cancellation for contracts on/after July 1, 2025; online cancel for online sign-ups predates it); FTC click-to-cancel rule vacated July 8, 2025; ROSCA still enforced. One sentence: 'counsel decides what applies to your contracts; design makes the path findable.' No legal advice, no claim about B2B applicability.
Hub fact: 'Plans and billing' covers pricing pages, upgrade prompts, usage limits, invoices and cancellation flows (paraphrase).
Bridge: 'A limit message is a system state; so are the blank, slow and broken screens covered next.'

outline.h2: What do empty, loading and error states owe a returning SaaS user?
outline.answerHint: **Every state a returning user can hit, from an empty filter result to a failed sync, owes them two things: what is happening and the one action that moves them on.**
points: NN/g 3 empty-state guidelines (eav 'empty states'), including no 'No records' while still loading.
State matrix (text table, data module 6): empty (never used), empty (filtered), loading, partial, error/failed sync, no permission.

First-run empty states and setup checklists belong to the onboarding service: one cross-hub link here, anchor 'SaaS onboarding design' → /services/saas-products/saas-onboarding-design/ (the post's only cross-hub link). Do NOT restate first-run patterns.
Errors: say what failed and keep the user's input (method; link nothing extra).
Bridge: 'States tell a user what just happened; loops give them a reason to come back tomorrow.'

outline.h2: Which retention loops bring SaaS users back without nagging?
outline.answerHint: **Retention loops bring SaaS users back when each message points to new work that matters to them, such as a mention, an approval or a change in their numbers, and stays quiet otherwise.**
points: NN/g indicators/validations/notifications (eav 'notifications'): choose by type, urgency and whether the user must act; a notification center plus a weekly digest for passive events.

Loops that come from the product's own data (method): assigned task, approval waiting, score/metric change, saved view with new rows. Examples from cases, facts only: TradeZella mentor mode (coach compares mentees' cumulative P&L), Mass Media Co. creative task cards with owner, due date and progress, Digno's personal score page tracking the score over time.
Metric: weekly active use and retention; tie to the hub's activation-and-retention framing (hub metaDescription/abstract). No unsourced retention statistics.
Bridge: 'In B2B products every one of these surfaces has two readers, the person who pays and the person who works.'

outline.h2: How does B2B SaaS design change roles, tables and billing?
outline.answerHint: **B2B SaaS design adds a second reader to every surface: the admin or buyer who controls seats, security and invoices, next to the member who does the daily work.**
points: Hyponym H2 for 'b2b saas design' (carrier in the first sentence).
Roles: admin console (members, roles, SSO, audit log); tables: shared saved views and exports; billing: seats, invoices for finance, upgrade approval by the admin (connect to H2 6).

Enterprise-grade security reviews (SSO, SCIM, audit logs, SOC 2 evidence, Section 508) are one sentence + one link to /industries/enterprise/ with anchor 'admin consoles that pass security reviews'. Do NOT rebuild the enterprise page's role-permission matrix or its SOC 2/508 content.
B2C contrast in one sentence: a single person is buyer and user, so cancellation and plan rules for consumers (H2 6) bite harder.
Bridge: 'With seven surfaces and two readers, you need a way to choose where to start.'

outline.h2: How do you rate your own UX design for SaaS, surface by surface?
outline.answerHint: **Rate your own UX design for SaaS by marking each of the 7 surfaces red, amber or green on one visible symptom and one metric, then fix the reddest surface first.**
points: Triage heat-map grid (visual 7 = image 5) + astext table with an empty 'your rating' column.
How to fill it in 30 minutes is NOT allowed (unsourced). Say instead: pull each metric from your analytics and support tickets, and watch 3 sessions per surface (method).
Pillar fact: one surface can be a project; onboarding, a dashboard, billing or a single workflow are common starting points (link /services/saas-products/ with anchor 'SaaS product design', once).

LEAD ANGLE 2 here, then the second UP link to the hub with a varied anchor (e.g. 'the six product parts we design', to /services/saas-products/saas-design-agency/#what-does-our-saas-design-agency-deliver; plain hub URL if fragments count as the same target).
Close with Faizan's one-sentence first-person recommendation, no label, no 'Bottom line' H2.

faqs.q: Is UX design for SaaS different from designing other web apps?
faqs.a: Yes. Subscription software adds patterns most web apps lack, such as trials, seats, roles, usage limits, plan upgrades and invoices, and each one is a point where a paying customer either moves on or leaves (hub section 1 fact). Keep it to 2–3 sentences.

faqs.q: Which SaaS surface should we fix first after onboarding?
faqs.a: The one your triage grid marks reddest: the surface with the worst metric and the most support tickets. Pillar fact: one surface can be a project, and onboarding, a dashboard, billing or a single workflow are common starting points.

faqs.q: Should every role see the same SaaS dashboard?
faqs.a: No. Each role should see the status and next actions it can act on; modules a role can never use stay hidden. Digno shows one score at organization, department and individual level, each with its own view.

faqs.q: Which US rules shape SaaS cancellation screens?
faqs.a: For consumer subscriptions, California's Automatic Renewal Law as amended by AB 2863 lets people who signed up online cancel online, and AB 2863 adds a same-medium rule for contracts from July 1, 2025. The FTC's click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025, but the FTC still enforces ROSCA. Your counsel decides what applies; design makes the cancel path findable.

faqs.q: How do you measure UX design for SaaS after launch?
faqs.a: Agree 2 or 3 metrics at kick-off, such as activation rate, time to first value and trial-to-paid conversion, and compare them before and after release (hub FAQ). Add the per-surface metric from the triage grid for the surface you changed.

visuals.idea: A product window in the center, 7 tiles around it (dashboard, roles and permissions, data tables, settings, plans and billing, system states, retention loops), each tile with its job and a small metric chip. A faded 'sign-up and first run' tile sits outside the ring, labeled 'covered by onboarding'. Text panel: table surface | job | metric.

Left: a dashboard with 12 equal cards and no hierarchy. Right: a status line, 'changed since your last visit', 3 next-action items and a drill-down link, with 5 numbered callouts. Text panel: the 5 callouts as a list.

The same project screen 3 times (admin, member, guest) with modules shown, disabled with a reason, or hidden; a 4th frame shows 'You need Editor access' with the admin's name and a Request access button. Text panel: table role | sees | can do | when blocked.

Top: a red 'Limit reached' banner, a dead end. Bottom: a 4-part message (what stopped, what still works, cost to continue, who approves) with a usage meter and a 'Ask your admin to upgrade' path for members. Text panel: ordered list of the 4 parts.

7 rows (surfaces) × columns: symptom you can see | metric to pull | first fix | your rating (red/amber/green swatches left blank to fill). Not a scorecard with points (chatbot-design used a scorecard). Text panel: the same table with an empty rating column.

CASE STUDIES (exact facts only): TradeZella: crowded interface hid key metrics; hard to learn; no onboarding guide (do NOT use this line, the onboarding silo already uses it); web and mobile inconsistent; compact widgets for win rate and profit factor; trader-arranged widgets; mentor mode; +40% user interaction, +25% user retention, +30% new customers, 4.7 Trustpilot. Mass Media Co.: separate tools → one platform; order screen updates estimated cost as items are added; single dashboard for open tasks, sales operations, recent tasks; creative task cards with owner, due date, progress; order processing efficiency +30%; 'order processing error rate 2+, reduced from 25%' (quote as written, do not convert to a percentage drop); task completion +3%. Digno: score at organization, department and individual level; My Digno Score page explains factors and trend. DO NOT use Digno's revenue 5x, 126% profits, 13:1 ROI or '50% scaling' (business results, not UX), nor any Vocable figure. Do not attribute any result to one surface alone. No quotes or testimonials (none of these three has a client quote).

DO NOT MIRROR (saasui.design and other competitors' wording): 'a route forward, not a dead end', 'reassure rather than sell', 'graceful denial', 'hub of many small, unrelated tasks', 'buyers approve, admins trust, users open', 'five core patterns', 'activation velocity'. Express the ideas in our own structure (4-part limit message with an approver, role lens, state matrix).

DO NOT USE (unsourced figures seen in SERP snippets): 'strong UX yields up to 400% higher conversion' (vendor blog), 'every $1 in UX returns $100', '88% of users won't return after a bad experience', any '% of SaaS churn is caused by UX' claim, Dribbble listing prices ('from $3,500', '$5,000 one month'), any 'users decide in N seconds' figure.
